rationale: I'm adding sample location (stool, terminal ileum or rectum) as one-hot features. Biopsy and stool communities differ a lot, so the forest currently has to learn disease signals from a mix of very different sample types; it should help to let it split on location first and then learn disease rules within each type (published AUROC is about 0.71 for stool versus 0.85 for biopsy). The metadata is matched to samples by index, or by position if the indices don't line up.

I'm adding OTU-level alpha-diversity features to the genus features the random forest already uses: observed richness, Shannon, inverse Simpson, Pielou evenness and genus richness. They are computed on counts rarefied to a common depth, so sequencing depth doesn't distort them. Lower within-sample diversity is one of the most consistent signs of dysbiosis in Crohn's disease, and summing to genus level hides it. It should also carry over to other stool studies, because diversity doesn't depend on study-specific OTU ids.

The current genus aggregation puts every OTU with an empty genus (`g__`) into one shared column, whatever family it belongs to. That mixes unclassified Lachnospiraceae/Ruminococcaceae, which are lost in Crohn's, with unclassified Enterobacteriaceae, which increase. I will instead aggregate by full lineage at every rank from phylum to genus, so unassigned taxa stay in their parent clade. This also adds family and phylum features, which match the published IBD signals and should transfer better across studies.

I'm dropping genera that are nonzero in fewer than 10% of the training samples, deciding this on each training fold without using labels. Most genus columns are rare and close to empty. A random forest that looks at only √p features at each split wastes most split candidates on these noise columns, and they also make the sample-location features less likely to be considered. Keeping only the reasonably common, transferable genera should make the trees more stable and improve the probability ranking. I haven't run this change, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Stool and mucosal biopsies have very different baseline communities. So I'm converting each genus's relative abundance into a percentile within its own sample location, using reference distributions from the training fold only. That lets "higher than usual for this sample type", the Crohn's dysbiosis signal, be split on directly, instead of the forest first having to find location splits (rarely chosen with √p features). It should also carry over to other stool studies, because their stool samples are ranked against stool references.

I'm keeping the random forest and averaging its probabilities with those of an L2 logistic regression on the same location-wise percentile features. The regularization strength is tuned by inner CV grouped by subject, using only the training fold. Crohn's dysbiosis looks like many small, consistent shifts (fewer Faecalibacterium and Roseburia, more Enterobacteriaceae and Fusobacterium), which a linear model sums directly and a forest only approximates. Combining the two models should rank samples better. This change hasn't been run, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding the Gevers 2014 microbial dysbiosis index as one extra feature. It is the log of (Enterobacteriaceae + Pasteurellaceae + Veillonellaceae + Fusobacteriaceae + Neisseriaceae + Gemellaceae) divided by (Bacteroidales + Clostridiales excluding Veillonellaceae + Erysipelotrichaceae + Bifidobacteriaceae). It goes through the same location-wise percentile step and always skips the prevalence filter. This pre-aggregated, published Crohn's signature pools many sparse, noisy taxa into one robust gradient. Neither the forest's √p splits nor a per-genus L2 model builds that kind of feature on its own, and because it uses names only it should carry over to the other stool studies.

Each subject contributes several samples, so a fully grown random forest (min_samples_leaf=1) can memorise subject-specific profiles in leaves of size 1, which gives overconfident, poorly ranked probabilities on unseen subjects. I'll choose min_samples_leaf from {1, 3, 5, 10} using subject-grouped inner CV on the training fold, then fit the final forest (1000 trees) with that value. This should smooth its probabilities and improve the RF+LR average.

The RF and LR probabilities are currently averaged with a fixed 50/50 weight. But RF probabilities shrink toward the base rate as min_samples_leaf grows, while LR's are more spread out, so the effective balance drifts with the tuned leaf size. I'll pick the RF weight from {0, 0.1, …, 1} using subject-grouped inner out-of-fold predictions from both models. The RF ones are reused from the leaf tuning, and ties are broken toward 0.5. This should give a better-ranked blend without touching the held-out folds. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

The logistic regression currently uses one coefficient per genus for every sample type, but Crohn's mucosal biopsies (terminal ileum, rectum) carry a stronger and partly different disease signal than stool. Published AUROC is about 0.85 for biopsies versus 0.71 for stool. I'll give the logistic regression an extra block of centred percentile × mucosal-indicator features, so each genus gets a shared effect plus a biopsy-specific adjustment. The tuned L2 penalty pulls those adjustments toward the shared effect, and the forest's inputs stay the same. Stool-only external studies would use only the shared effects.

I'm adding a third model, a shallow, heavily regularized LightGBM, and averaging its probabilities equally with the RF and LR. Its number of boosting rounds is picked by subject-grouped inner CV on the training fold. Crohn's dysbiosis comes from many small genus shifts (which the LR sums) plus threshold and interaction effects that depend on location (which the RF approximates). Boosting fits these additive-plus-interaction effects step by step on the residuals, so it should add a different kind of error and improve the ranking of the blend. I haven't run this change, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

The forest only looks at √p genera (about 10) at each split, so many splits end up on weak genera even when a strong Crohn's marker like Enterobacteriaceae, Faecalibacterium or Fusobacterium is available. I'll choose max_features from {sqrt, 0.33} together with min_samples_leaf, using the same subject-grouped inner CV on the training fold. If the strong markers are being under-used, the forest's ranking should improve. This hasn't been run, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

The logistic regression will use log relative abundance (pseudocount 1e-4), standardized within each sample location using training-fold statistics, in place of percentiles; the random forest keeps its percentile features. Percentiles flatten the large fold changes typical of Crohn's dysbiosis (for example Enterobacteriaceae blooms and Faecalibacterium loss), which a log scale captures. Giving the two models different views of the data should also make their errors less alike, improving the blend.

The logistic regression will also get family-level log relative abundances, with the same location-wise standardization, alongside the genus features it already uses. The random forest keeps only genus-level percentiles. Much of the published Crohn's signal sits at family level (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae up; Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae down) and is spread across sparse genera and unclassified `g__` OTUs. Family sums pool those into denser, less noisy signals that an L2 model can weight directly, and they should transfer better to other studies. Round 3 did a full-lineage aggregation for the forest, which is not the same change.

Many subjects contribute several samples (stool plus ileal and rectal biopsies), so subjects with many samples dominate both the forest's splits and the logistic regression's loss. That pushes both models towards subject-specific profiles rather than disease signal shared across subjects. I'll weight each training sample by 1/(number of that subject's samples in the training fold), normalised to mean 1. The weights are used in RF tuning, the final RF and the logistic regression, and should help the models generalise to unseen subjects and to other cohorts.

Grouped inner CV on the training fold will now choose between ExtraTrees and the current random forest, alongside min_samples_leaf and max_features. Each subject contributes several near-duplicate samples, so the forest's best-split thresholds can fit subject-specific abundance cut-offs. ExtraTrees pick split thresholds at random, which should give lower-variance, smoother probabilities that rank unseen subjects better. I haven't run this, so there's no Dev score for it yet.

The logistic regression will use centred log-ratio (CLR) transformed genus abundances: each sample's log relative abundances minus their per-sample mean, over the prevalence-filtered genera, then standardized within each sample location as now. In Crohn's disease a single taxon can bloom (for example Enterobacteriaceae), which pushes down every other genus's relative abundance and makes them all look depleted at once. CLR measures each genus against the sample's geometric mean instead, which removes that artefact and should give a cleaner multiplicative signal that also transfers better to other studies.

I'm adding a beta-diversity "dysbiosis distance" block, built only from training-fold labels. For each sample I compute the median Bray-Curtis distance on genus profiles to the training controls and, separately, to the training Crohn's samples of the same sample location, plus the difference between the two. For training samples, references from the same subject are left out, so their features are computed the same way as for unseen subjects. Crohn's dysbiosis is a shift of the whole community away from the healthy reference, as in Gevers and Halfvarson. Per-genus percentiles or logs don't capture that, while a community-level distance does, and it doesn't depend on study-specific OTU ids. The new features go to both models: percentile-normalized for the random forest and z-scored for the logistic regression.

The logistic regression currently uses a fixed pseudocount of 1e-4 on relative abundance, but sequencing depth varies a lot, so a zero means different things in different samples. In a 2,000-read sample a genus can be up to 5e-4 and still read zero; in a 50,000-read sample it can only be up to 2e-5. I'll use a per-sample pseudocount of half a read (0.5/depth) for the LR log features, which puts zeros at each sample's own detection limit. This removes depth-driven spread from the log-abundance features, should help transfer to studies with different depths, and leaves the RF unchanged.

Round 19 showed that a depth-aware pseudocount, which places each zero at that sample's own detection limit (0.5 reads/depth), improves the logistic regression. The random forest still ranks raw relative abundance, so all zeros tie at one percentile, whether the sample had 2,000 reads or 50,000. I'll make the forest's location-wise percentiles use the same depth-aware log relative abundance. A zero in a deeply sequenced sample then ranks below a zero in a shallow one, so the forest can tell a confident absence (such as Faecalibacterium loss) from missing data at low depth.
